section_title: Why does God end the warning with an invitation to live?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 30 Therefore, O house of Israel, I will judge you, each according to his ways, declares the Lord GOD. Repent and turn from all your transgressions, so that your iniquity will not become your downfall. 31 Cast away from yourselves all the transgressions you have committed, and fashion for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit. Why should you die, O house of Israel? 32 For I take no pleasure in anyone’s death, declares the Lord GOD. So repent and live!

context_lines: The Lord brings the chapter’s examples into a direct appeal. He will judge each person according to that person’s ways, so the people must turn away from their transgressions before iniquity becomes their downfall.
They are called to cast away their offenses and have a new heart and spirit. The final question asks why Israel should die, and the Lord declares that He takes no pleasure in anyone’s death.

The warning serves the invitation: repent and live. They receive an urgent invitation to respond, rather than being left with the claim that their ancestors or past actions have made the future meaningless.
common_interpretation_lines: [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/ezekiel/18.htm) understands the appeal as a call to use the means God provides and seek from Him the inward change that is needed. [Wesley](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/ezekiel/18.htm) likewise explains the new-heart command as allowing God to do His work within the people.

[Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/18.htm) also notes that the Lord elsewhere promises to give the new heart. He reads the immediate warning in terms of the calamity facing Israel and stresses sincere repentance. These readings connect the required response with God’s provision, rather than imagining that a new heart is created by an outward performance alone.
god_plan_lines: [Hebrews 3:7–14](https://biblehub.com/bsb/hebrews/3.htm) takes up the danger of a hardened heart and calls believers to encourage one another today, so that sin’s deception does not draw them away from the living God.

[Second Peter 3:8–14](https://biblehub.com/bsb/2_peter/3.htm) explains God’s patience in relation to repentance and the promised new creation. The time before judgment is an opportunity to turn and live faithfully as His people look toward a world where righteousness dwells.

Neither passage explicitly quotes Ezekiel 18. Together they develop the larger purpose behind its invitation: God’s warning calls for a present response, and His patience gives room for repentance rather than making sin harmless.
